learningShell.prose:
A block is a fixed-width sequence of bits. The same value can be written in binary or hexadecimal: every hexadecimal digit represents four bits, and two digits represent one byte. Leading zeroes remain part of the block even when they do not change its numerical value.

Exclusive OR combines bits at the same position. Equal inputs produce zero; different inputs produce one. Applying the same key twice restores the original value, because each key bit cancels its earlier contribution.

### Reading the state

For a 128-bit block, the state contains sixteen bytes. Byte boundaries help us group the value without changing the order of its bits. The first byte is still the first byte whether the entire state is written as bits, bytes, or one hexadecimal string.
learningShell.after: The initial AddRoundKey combines the plaintext with the first 128 key bits. The key size determines the later key schedule; the cipher state remains 128 bits wide.
